Ransomware
Spyware
questions.explain: A logic bomb is code that lies dormant until a set condition, here the disabling of his account, then runs its payload. A backdoor gives hidden access but does not wait to destroy data. A worm spreads itself, ransomware encrypts data for payment, and spyware secretly collects information.

questions.stem: Malware changes the operating system kernel so its own files and processes no longer appear in Task Manager or directory listings, and antivirus running inside the operating system reports the machine as clean. What is it?
options: Rootkit
Keylogger
Worm
Adware
Trojan horse
questions.explain: A rootkit hides itself and other malware by changing the operating system at a deep level, such as the kernel or boot process, so tools that trust the operating system cannot see it. A trojan horse describes how malware gets installed, not how it hides. A keylogger records keystrokes, a worm spreads itself, and adware shows unwanted ads.

questions.stem: An attack runs entirely in memory through PowerShell and WMI and never writes a malicious program to disk. Why does it often get past traditional antivirus?
options: Signature scanners mainly check files on disk, and there is no malicious file to scan
Windows encrypts PowerShell scripts, so scanners cannot read them
The operating system automatically trusts any code running in memory
It always deletes the antivirus program before it starts
No security tool is able to log commands that run in memory
questions.explain: Fileless malware abuses tools already on the system and lives in memory, so a scanner that looks for known bad files has nothing to match. PowerShell scripts are not encrypted by default, and memory-resident code is not automatically trusted. Behavior-based tools such as EDR and PowerShell logging can record this activity, so the claim that nothing can log it is false.

questions.stem: Thousands of infected home routers sit quietly until a remote server tells them to flood a target with traffic at the same moment. What is that remote server called?
options: Command-and-control (C2) server
DNS resolver
Proxy server
Honeypot
Domain controller
questions.explain: The infected devices form a botnet, and the server that sends them orders is its command-and-control server. A DNS resolver turns names into addresses, and a proxy forwards traffic for clients. A honeypot is a decoy built by defenders, and a domain controller handles logins on a Windows domain.

questions.stem: A user downloads a free PDF converter that works exactly as advertised but also quietly opens a remote-access connection for an attacker. How is this malware best classified?
options: Trojan horse
Worm
Virus
Logic bomb
Rootkit
questions.explain: A trojan horse is malware disguised as, or bundled with, a useful program that the user installs willingly. A worm spreads without user action and a virus attaches itself to other files. A logic bomb waits for a trigger, and a rootkit's defining feature is hiding, which the stem does not describe.

questions.stem: An attacker studies a company's chief financial officer online, then sends her a tailored email that appears to come from the CEO and demands an urgent wire transfer. Which term most precisely describes this attack?
options: Whaling
Vishing
Smishing
Pharming
Baiting
questions.explain: Whaling is targeted phishing aimed at a senior executive, which is exactly this. Vishing uses voice calls and smishing uses text messages. Pharming redirects users to fake sites through DNS or host-file tampering, and baiting leaves a lure such as an infected USB drive for someone to pick up.

questions.stem: A caller says he is from the help desk fixing an email outage and asks an airman to read back the six-digit code that was just texted to her phone. What is he most likely trying to do?
options: Get past her account's multifactor authentication
Install a keylogger on her phone
Reset the help desk's own admin password
Poison the base DNS cache
Confirm that her number is active for spam
questions.explain: The texted code is a one-time second factor, so an attacker who already has her password needs it to finish logging in as her. Reading a code aloud cannot install software, reset someone else's password or change DNS records. Confirming a number for spam would not need a live code from a login attempt.

questions.stem: A person without a badge, carrying two boxes of printer paper, waits by a secure door and walks in when an employee holds it open for him. Which control is built specifically to stop this?
options: An access control vestibule (mantrap) that admits one person per badge
Security cameras covering the entrance
A longer and more complex password policy
Badge readers on both sides of the door
A visitor sign-in log at the front desk
questions.explain: Tailgating is stopped physically by a vestibule or turnstile that lets only one badged person through at a time. Cameras record the event but do not prevent it. Badge readers and a visitor log do nothing when someone simply holds the door, and a password policy has nothing to do with physical entry.

questions.stem: An attacker phones a records office posing as a new auditor from headquarters, uses real names and an invented audit deadline, and talks staff into emailing personnel files. The invented story is the core of which technique?
options: Pretexting
Baiting
Quid pro quo
Shoulder surfing
Dumpster diving
questions.explain: Pretexting means building a believable made-up scenario and role to get information. Baiting uses a lure such as a free download or a found USB drive, and quid pro quo offers a service in exchange for information. Shoulder surfing and dumpster diving collect information by watching people or searching trash, not by talking them into anything.

questions.stem: A login page builds its database query by pasting whatever the user types straight into the SQL statement. Which defense most directly prevents SQL injection?
options: Parameterized queries (prepared statements)
Hashing stored passwords with a salt
Requiring HTTPS on the login page
Hiding database error messages from users
Limiting each user to five login attempts
questions.explain: Parameterized queries send user input to the database as data, never as part of the SQL command, so injected code cannot run. Salting protects stored passwords and HTTPS protects data in transit, but neither changes how the query is built. Hiding errors makes injection harder to tune but does not stop it, and login limits do not stop a single successful injection.

questions.stem: Typing  ' OR '1'='1' --  into a username field logs an attacker in without a password. Why does this work?
options: The added condition is always true and the comment marker cuts off the password check
The quote mark crashes the database, which then lets everyone in
It matches a default administrator account built into SQL
The comment marker encrypts the rest of the query
It overflows the username buffer and overwrites the password
questions.explain: The quote closes the username string, OR '1'='1' makes the WHERE clause true for every row, and -- turns the rest of the query, including the password check, into a comment. Databases do not fail open on a stray quote, and SQL has no built-in account by that name. A comment marker hides code rather than encrypting it, and this is an injection, not a memory overflow.

questions.stem: A forum shows user comments without filtering them. An attacker posts a comment containing a script that sends each reader's session cookie to his server. What is this attack?
options: Stored cross-site scripting
Reflected cross-site scripting
Cross-site request forgery
SQL injection
Directory traversal
questions.explain: The script is saved on the site and runs in the browser of everyone who views the page, which is stored, or persistent, XSS. Reflected XSS bounces a script off the site in a single crafted request, such as a link, and is not saved. CSRF forges requests rather than running script, SQL injection targets the database, and directory traversal reaches files outside the web folder.

questions.stem: While logged in to her bank, a user opens a malicious page that silently submits a funds-transfer form to the bank using her existing session. Which defense is designed for this attack?
options: Unique anti-CSRF tokens in each form
Output encoding of user comments
Parameterized database queries
Address space layout randomization
Turning off the browser's autocomplete
questions.explain: This is cross-site request forgery, and a secret token the attacker's page cannot know makes the forged form fail. Output encoding defends against XSS and parameterized queries against SQL injection. ASLR is a memory protection against exploits such as buffer overflows, and autocomplete settings do not affect requests sent with an existing session.

questions.stem: A program copies a 300-byte input into a 64-byte array without checking the length, letting an attacker overwrite the function's return address. Which protection makes it much harder for the attacker to know where to send execution?
options: Address space layout randomization (ASLR)
Data loss prevention (DLP)
Salting stored passwords
Network address translation (NAT)
Transport Layer Security (TLS)
questions.explain: ASLR places code and data at random memory addresses each time a program runs, so the attacker cannot reliably predict where his payload or useful code sits. DLP watches for sensitive data leaving the network, and salting protects password hashes. NAT rewrites network addresses and TLS encrypts traffic, and neither affects memory layout on the target.

questions.stem: On a switched LAN, an attacker sends forged replies telling every host that the default gateway's IP address belongs to his own MAC address. What attack is this, and what does it let him do?
options: ARP spoofing, letting him intercept traffic as a man in the middle
DNS poisoning, redirecting a domain name to his server
MAC flooding, forcing the switch to act like a hub
IP spoofing, hiding the true source of a DDoS
DHCP starvation, using up the address pool
questions.explain: ARP maps IP addresses to MAC addresses on a local network, and forged ARP replies make hosts send gateway traffic to the attacker, who can read or change it before passing it on. DNS poisoning forges name records, not MAC mappings. MAC flooding overfills the switch table, IP spoofing fakes a source address, and DHCP starvation exhausts leases.

questions.stem: An attacker records a valid, encrypted login exchange and later sends it again unchanged to get in, without ever decrypting it. Which countermeasure defeats this?
options: Nonces or timestamps that make each exchange valid only once
Longer encryption keys
Switching the cipher from RSA to AES
Hashing the password before it is sent
Moving the server into a DMZ
questions.explain: This is a replay attack, and a one-time value or a short time window makes a recorded exchange worthless when sent again. Stronger keys or a different cipher do not help because the attacker never decrypts anything. A password hash sent the same way every time can itself be replayed, and a DMZ changes network placement, not the login protocol.

questions.stem: Users who type a bank's correct web address are sent to a fake site because a DNS resolver stored a forged record. Which technology lets resolvers verify DNS answers with digital signatures?
options: DNSSEC
DNS over HTTPS
DHCP snooping
SNMPv3
Split-horizon DNS
questions.explain: DNSSEC adds digital signatures to DNS records so a resolver can check that an answer came from the real zone and was not altered. DNS over HTTPS encrypts the query between a client and its resolver but does not prove the records themselves are genuine. DHCP snooping blocks rogue DHCP servers, SNMPv3 secures device management, and split-horizon DNS gives different answers to inside and outside users.

questions.stem: An attacker sends thousands of TCP SYN packets with spoofed source addresses and never completes the three-way handshake. Which resource on the server is he trying to exhaust?
options: Its table of half-open connections
Its disk space for log files
The switch's MAC address table
The DHCP address pool
The DNS resolver's cache
questions.explain: Each SYN makes the server reserve a slot and wait for the final ACK that never comes, so the half-open connection table fills and real users are refused. Log space can grow but is not the target. The MAC table, DHCP pool and DNS cache belong to other attacks: MAC flooding, DHCP starvation and DNS poisoning.

questions.stem: At an airport, a laptop joins a Wi-Fi network with the same name as the airline lounge, but the signal actually comes from an attacker's device placed nearby. What is the attacker's access point called?
options: Evil twin
Rogue access point
War driving
Bluejacking
MAC flooding
questions.explain: An evil twin copies a legitimate network's SSID to trick users into connecting so the attacker can watch their traffic. A rogue access point is an unauthorized access point plugged into an organization's own network, often by an employee, not one built to impersonate a known network. War driving is searching for networks, bluejacking sends unwanted Bluetooth messages, and MAC flooding attacks switches.

questions.stem: Why can't a signature-based intrusion detection system reliably catch a zero-day exploit?
options: No signature exists yet, because the flaw is not known to the vendor or defenders
Zero-day exploits always arrive inside encrypted traffic
Signature-based systems inspect only outbound traffic
Zero-day attacks target hardware, which an IDS cannot see
The IDS must be rebooted before it can load any new rule
questions.explain: A zero-day exploits a flaw before it is publicly known or patched, so there is no pattern for a signature system to match. Some zero-days travel unencrypted, and signature systems can inspect traffic in both directions. Most zero-days target software, and new rules are loaded without a reboot.

questions.stem: After a breach at an online store, attackers try the leaked email and password pairs on banking websites, and many of them work. What is this attack called?
options: Credential stuffing
Password spraying
Brute-force attack
Rainbow table attack
Pass the hash
questions.explain: Credential stuffing replays known username and password pairs from one breach on other sites, betting that people reuse passwords. Password spraying tries a few common passwords across many accounts, and brute force tries every combination. A rainbow table cracks stolen hashes offline, and pass the hash reuses a captured hash on Windows networks.

questions.stem: An attacker tries one common password against each of 4,000 user accounts, then waits an hour before trying a second password. Why does he work this way?
options: To stay under each account's lockout threshold
To get around the salt on each password hash
To build a rainbow table for the domain
To keep the help desk from resetting passwords
To avoid filling up the server's session table
questions.explain: This is password spraying: a few attempts per account, spread over time, never trip the lockout that would follow many quick failures on one account. Salts matter only when cracking stolen hashes offline, which this online attack does not do. Rainbow tables are built offline, and the slow pace is not about help-desk resets or session tables.

questions.stem: Two users chose exactly the same password, yet on a well-designed system their stored password hashes are different. Why?
options: Each password was combined with its own random salt before hashing
Each password was encrypted with that user's public key
The system uses MD5, which gives random output each time
Each hash was cut to a different length for each user
The passwords were hashed at different times of day
questions.explain: A unique salt added before hashing makes identical passwords produce different hashes, which defeats rainbow tables and hides reused passwords. Passwords are hashed, not encrypted with public keys. MD5, like any hash, always gives the same output for the same input, and neither truncation nor the time of day changes a hash.

questions.stem: A system allows passwords of exactly 8 characters, each one of 26 lowercase letters. If the rule changes to exactly 9 characters from the same set, the number of possible passwords is multiplied by
questions.explain: There are 26 to the 8th power possible 8-character passwords and 26 to the 9th power possible 9-character ones, so the extra position multiplies the total by 26. Nine and eight confuse the length with the growth, 2 would mean the space only doubles, and 234 is 26 times 9, which mixes the two numbers.

questions.stem: A team of 10 people wants every pair to talk privately with symmetric encryption, using a different key for each pair. How many keys are needed?
questions.explain: Each pair needs one shared key, and 10 people make 10 times 9 divided by 2, or 45 pairs. Twenty is the number of keys an asymmetric system would need (a public and a private key each). Ninety counts every pair twice, and 10 and 100 do not count pairs at all.

questions.stem: Using public-key cryptography, Alice wants only Bob to be able to read her message. Which key does she encrypt it with?
options: Bob's public key
Bob's private key
Alice's private key
Alice's public key
A session key she sends to Bob by email first
questions.explain: Anything encrypted with Bob's public key can be decrypted only with Bob's private key, which only he holds. Alice never has Bob's private key. Encrypting with her own private key creates a signature anyone can check, encrypting with her own public key means only she can read it, and emailing a session key in the clear gives it away.

questions.stem: To digitally sign a document, the sender
options: encrypts a hash of the document with her own private key
encrypts the whole document with the recipient's public key
encrypts a hash of the document with the recipient's public key
hashes the document using her own public key
encrypts the document with a key she shares with the recipient
questions.explain: A signature is a hash of the document processed with the signer's private key, and anyone can check it with her public key. Encrypting with the recipient's public key gives confidentiality, not proof of who sent it. Public keys do not create signatures, and a shared key cannot prove which of the two holders signed.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly tells hashing apart from encryption?
options: Hashing is one-way with a fixed-length output, while encryption can be reversed with the right key
Hashing needs a key to reverse it, while encryption does not
Hashing protects confidentiality, while encryption protects integrity
A hash grows with the size of the input, while ciphertext does not
Hashing is used only for passwords, while encryption is used only for files
questions.explain: A hash function turns any input into a fixed-length digest that cannot be turned back into the input, while encryption is designed to be decrypted by whoever holds the key. The second option swaps the usual roles: hashes check integrity and encryption gives confidentiality. Ciphertext, not a hash, grows with the input, and both tools have many uses beyond passwords and files.

questions.stem: In an HTTPS session, why is most of the data encrypted with a symmetric cipher such as AES rather than with RSA?
options: Symmetric encryption is far faster, so asymmetric methods are used only to authenticate and set up the session key
RSA can encrypt only one character at a time
Symmetric ciphers are stronger than every asymmetric cipher at any key length
Browsers are not allowed to store RSA public keys
AES is the only cipher that can run over TCP
questions.explain: TLS is a hybrid: public-key methods prove the server's identity and agree on a shared session key, then fast symmetric encryption protects the bulk data. RSA can encrypt more than a character but is much slower. Strength depends on key length and algorithm, not just type, and browsers do handle public keys in certificates. Ciphers do not depend on TCP.

questions.stem: A web browser trusts a site's TLS certificate mainly because
options: it is signed by a certificate authority whose root certificate the browser already trusts
it contains the website's private key
the site's IP address matches its DNS record
it was downloaded over port 443
it uses a 256-bit hash algorithm
questions.explain: Trust comes from the chain of signatures leading back to a root CA in the browser's trusted store. A certificate holds the public key, never the private key. Matching DNS, using port 443 or a strong hash do not show that a trusted authority vouched for the site, and a self-signed certificate can have all three and still trigger a warning.

questions.stem: Which login is true two-factor authentication?
options: A smart card plus the PIN that unlocks it
A password plus the answer to a security question
A fingerprint scan plus a palm scan
A password plus a separate PIN
Two different passwords for two systems
questions.explain: Two-factor authentication needs two different factor types, and a smart card (something you have) plus a PIN (something you know) qualifies, which is how a CAC works. A password with a security answer or a PIN is two things you know. Fingerprint and palm are both something you are, and two passwords are still one factor.

questions.stem: When comparing biometric systems, what does a lower crossover error rate (CER) show?
options: Better overall accuracy at the point where false acceptances equal false rejections
Faster enrollment of new users
Fewer false rejections but more false acceptances
That the system is tuned for the highest security
That it reads more points on each fingerprint
questions.explain: The CER is the rate at which the false acceptance and false rejection rates are equal, and a lower CER means a more accurate system overall. It says nothing about enrollment speed or how many fingerprint points are read. Trading false rejections for false acceptances, or tuning for maximum security, moves the system away from the crossover point.

questions.stem: Users on a Windows domain suddenly cannot log in, and the logs show Kerberos errors. The domain controller's clock is 20 minutes behind the workstations. Why does that matter?
options: Kerberos tickets carry timestamps, and too much clock difference makes them invalid
Kerberos uses the current time as the encryption key
Password hashes expire after 15 minutes
DNS records refresh only when clocks match
The certificate authority rejects requests from slow clocks
questions.explain: Kerberos puts timestamps in its tickets and authenticators to block replays, and by default it rejects anything more than about 5 minutes out of step. The time is not the key, password hashes do not expire on a timer, and DNS refresh does not depend on matching clocks. Kerberos uses a key distribution center, not a certificate authority.

questions.stem: What is the main security trade-off of single sign-on (SSO)?
options: One stolen credential can unlock every connected system
Users have to remember more passwords
It cannot be combined with multifactor authentication
Each application must keep its own copy of the password
It works only with applications on the local network
questions.explain: SSO lets one login reach many systems, so a compromised account exposes all of them, which is why SSO is usually paired with strong MFA. It reduces, not increases, the number of passwords. It works with MFA and with cloud services, and applications trust the identity provider instead of storing their own password copies.

questions.stem: A central authority gives every file a classification label and every user a clearance, and file owners cannot change who may read their files. Which access control model is this?
options: Mandatory access control (MAC)
Discretionary access control (DAC)
Role-based access control (RBAC)
Attribute-based access control (ABAC)
Rule-based access control
questions.explain: MAC compares labels set by a central authority with users' clearances, and owners cannot override it. In DAC the owner decides who gets access. RBAC grants access by job role, ABAC by combinations of attributes such as department and location, and rule-based control applies fixed rules, such as a firewall rule list, to everyone.

questions.stem: One finance clerk can both create a new vendor in the payment system and approve payments to that vendor. Which principle does this most directly violate?
options: Separation of duties
Need to know
Job rotation
Implicit deny
Defense in depth
questions.explain: Separation of duties splits a sensitive process so no one person can complete it alone, and creating and paying a vendor is the classic fraud risk. Need to know limits access to information, and job rotation moves staff between roles to expose fraud. Implicit deny blocks anything not explicitly allowed, and defense in depth layers controls.

questions.stem: A policy lets a user open the payroll application only if she works in finance, is on a government-issued device and connects during duty hours. Which access control model does this describe?
options: Attribute-based access control (ABAC)
Role-based access control (RBAC)
Discretionary access control (DAC)
Mandatory access control (MAC)
Identity federation
questions.explain: ABAC decides access by evaluating several attributes of the user, the device and the conditions together. RBAC checks only the user's role, DAC leaves the decision to the data owner, and MAC compares classification labels with clearances. Identity federation lets one organization trust another's logins, which is not an access model.

questions.stem: An analyst holds a Secret clearance and has signed his nondisclosure agreement. What else must be true before he may read a particular Secret report?
options: He needs the information to do his official duties
He must also hold a Top Secret clearance
The report must first be lowered to Confidential
His supervisor must hold the same clearance
He must read it on a personally owned device
questions.explain: Access to classified information takes the right clearance, a signed nondisclosure agreement and a need to know, so a clearance alone is not enough. A Secret clearance already covers Secret material, and the report does not need to be downgraded. His supervisor's clearance is irrelevant, and classified material must never be viewed on a personal device.

questions.stem: What is the key difference between an intrusion detection system (IDS) and an intrusion prevention system (IPS)?
options: An IPS sits inline and can block traffic, while an IDS monitors and alerts
An IDS sits inline and blocks traffic, while an IPS only alerts
An IDS uses signatures, while an IPS uses only anomaly detection
An IPS is always software, while an IDS is always hardware
An IDS protects one host, while an IPS protects a whole network
questions.explain: An IPS is placed in the traffic path so it can drop malicious packets, while an IDS watches a copy of traffic and raises alerts. The second option reverses them. Both can use signature and anomaly methods, both come as hardware or software, and both exist in host-based and network-based forms.

questions.stem: Compared with signature-based detection, anomaly-based detection is better at catching ______ but tends to produce more ______.
options: new, unknown attacks; false positives
known malware; false negatives
new, unknown attacks; false negatives
known malware; false positives
encrypted traffic; dropped packets
questions.explain: Anomaly detection learns what normal looks like and flags anything unusual, so it can catch attacks no one has a signature for, but unusual legitimate activity also trips it. Signature systems are the ones that excel at known malware. More false negatives would mean missing more attacks, which is the opposite of anomaly detection's strength, and it does not decrypt traffic.

questions.stem: A firewall lets an inbound packet through only if it belongs to a connection that an inside host already started. What type of firewall is this?
options: Stateful inspection firewall
Stateless packet-filtering firewall
Web application firewall
Network-based IDS
Honeypot
questions.explain: A stateful firewall keeps a table of active connections and allows return traffic that matches one. A stateless packet filter judges each packet on its own header fields with no memory of earlier packets. A web application firewall inspects HTTP requests to a web app, an IDS alerts rather than filters, and a honeypot is a decoy.

questions.stem: A unit runs a public email server. Which network design means that, if the email server is compromised, the attacker still has to get through a firewall to reach internal systems?
options: A screened subnet (DMZ)
A flat network
An air gap
A honeynet
Split tunneling
questions.explain: A screened subnet places public-facing servers in their own zone with firewall rules between it and the internal network. A flat network puts everything on one segment, so nothing stands in the way. An air-gapped server could not serve the public at all, a honeynet is a set of decoys, and split tunneling is a VPN routing setting.

questions.stem: A server with fake data and no real business use is placed on the network to attract attackers so defenders can study their methods. What is it?
options: Honeypot
Sandbox
Bastion host
Jump box
Proxy server
questions.explain: A honeypot is a deliberate decoy whose only value is being attacked and watched. A sandbox runs suspicious code in isolation, and a bastion host is a real, hardened server exposed to the internet. A jump box is the controlled entry point admins use to reach secure systems, and a proxy forwards traffic for clients.

questions.stem: A unit protects a server with an edge firewall, host-based firewalls, MFA, full-disk encryption, EDR and locked server rooms, so an attacker who gets past one control still faces the others. Which principle is this?
options: Defense in depth
Least privilege
Separation of duties
Zero trust
Security through obscurity
questions.explain: Defense in depth layers independent physical, technical and administrative controls so one failure does not expose the asset. Least privilege limits each account to the permissions its job needs, and separation of duties splits a sensitive task between people. Zero trust means never trusting a request because of its network location and verifying every access, which can use layers but is a different principle. Obscurity relies on hiding how a system works.

questions.stem: An unpatched web server, a criminal group scanning the internet for that flaw, and the chance that they break in and leak data are, in that order,
options: a vulnerability, a threat and a risk
a threat, a vulnerability and a risk
a risk, a threat and an exploit
an exploit, a threat and a vulnerability
a vulnerability, an exploit and a threat
questions.explain: A vulnerability is a weakness (the missing patch), a threat is something that could use it (the group), and risk is the likelihood and impact of that happening (the chance of a breach). An exploit is the specific code or technique that uses a vulnerability, and none of the three items in the stem is an exploit.

questions.stem: A server worth $200,000 would lose 25 percent of its value in a flood, and a flood is expected once every 5 years. What is the annualized loss expectancy (ALE)?
questions.explain: The single loss expectancy is $200,000 times 0.25, or $50,000. Once every 5 years is an annual rate of 0.2, so the ALE is $50,000 times 0.2, or $10,000. $50,000 stops at the single loss, $40,000 skips the 25 percent, $250,000 multiplies by 5 instead of dividing, and $12,500 divides by 4.

questions.stem: A unit stops collecting Social Security numbers on an event sign-up form because it never needed them. Which risk response is this?
options: Risk avoidance
Risk mitigation
Risk transference
Risk acceptance
Risk deterrence
questions.explain: Avoidance removes the risk by ending the activity that creates it: data never collected cannot be leaked. Mitigation would keep collecting the numbers but protect them better, and transference shifts the cost to someone else, as insurance does. Acceptance means living with the risk, and deterrence is a type of control, not one of the risk responses.

questions.stem: In the NIST incident response life cycle, which phase comes immediately after detection and analysis?
options: Containment, eradication and recovery
Preparation
Post-incident activity
Lessons learned
Identification
questions.explain: The NIST life cycle runs preparation, then detection and analysis, then containment, eradication and recovery, then post-incident activity. Preparation comes first, and post-incident activity, which includes the lessons-learned review, comes last. Identification is a step name from other frameworks and overlaps with detection, which has already happened.

questions.stem: A workstation is sending regular beacons to a known malicious server. To contain it while preserving evidence, what should the responder do first?
options: Disconnect it from the network but leave it powered on
Shut it down immediately
Reimage it from the standard build
Run a full antivirus scan and delete what it finds
Reboot it into safe mode
questions.explain: Cutting the network link stops the beaconing and any spread, while keeping power preserves memory, which may hold the malware, keys and connections. Shutting down or rebooting wipes that volatile evidence. Reimaging and deleting files destroy evidence before anyone has analyzed it.

questions.stem: Following the order of volatility, which evidence should be collected first?
options: Contents of system memory (RAM)
Files on the hard drive
Archived backup tapes
Records on a remote syslog server
Printed network diagrams
questions.explain: Evidence is collected from most to least volatile, and RAM is lost the moment the machine loses power. Disk files survive a shutdown, remote logs are stored elsewhere and last longer still, and backup tapes and printed documents are the most stable of all.

questions.stem: Why is a chain-of-custody form kept for a seized hard drive?
options: To record everyone who handled it and when, so it can be used as evidence
To record the drive's encryption key
To track its warranty and serial number for repairs
To show the drive was wiped before disposal
To prove its hash will change after analysis
questions.explain: A chain of custody documents every transfer and handler so investigators can show the evidence was not tampered with. Keys are never written on custody forms, and warranty tracking is asset management. Wiping is recorded in a sanitization record, and analysts work on copies precisely so the original's hash does not change.

questions.stem: A full backup runs Sunday night and differential backups run Monday through Thursday nights. The server fails Friday morning. Which backups are needed to restore it?
options: Sunday's full backup and Thursday's differential
Sunday's full backup and all four differentials
Thursday's differential only
Sunday's full backup only
Monday's and Thursday's differentials
questions.explain: Each differential holds every change since the last full backup, so the full backup plus the newest differential restores everything. Needing every backup since the full is how incremental backups work. A differential alone has no base to apply to, the full backup alone loses four days of work, and Monday's differential adds nothing Thursday's does not already hold.

questions.stem: Which plan follows the 3-2-1 backup rule?
options: Three copies of the data, on two different types of media, with one copy offsite
Three copies, two of them offsite, all on one type of media
Three daily incrementals, two weekly fulls and one monthly archive
Three copies in one server room, on two disks, with one encrypted
Three backup servers, two network paths and one tape library
questions.explain: The 3-2-1 rule means three copies (the original plus two backups), on at least two kinds of media, with at least one stored offsite. One media type misses the second rule, and one server room misses the offsite rule. The other two options count backup jobs or hardware, not copies of the data.

questions.stem: Unauthorized disclosure of information that could reasonably be expected to cause serious damage to national security is classified at which level?
options: Secret
Top Secret
Confidential
Controlled Unclassified Information
For Official Use Only
questions.explain: Under Executive Order 13526, Secret covers serious damage, Top Secret covers exceptionally grave damage, and Confidential covers damage. Controlled Unclassified Information is not classified at all, and For Official Use Only is an older unclassified marking that CUI has largely replaced.

questions.stem: Which statement about Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI) is correct?
options: It is unclassified but still requires safeguarding and limits on who receives it
It is the lowest classified level, just below Confidential
Viewing it requires at least a Secret clearance
Once it is marked, it may be posted publicly
It covers only information owned by private companies
questions.explain: CUI is government-created or government-owned information that is not classified but that law, regulation or policy says must be protected and shared only with authorized people. It is not a classification level and needs no clearance. Marking it CUI is a warning not to release it publicly, and it is mostly government information, though contractors who handle it must protect it too.

questions.stem: A document that every user signs, stating what they may and may not do with government computers, email and internet access, is the
options: acceptable use policy
service level agreement
memorandum of understanding
nondisclosure agreement
business continuity plan
questions.explain: An acceptable use policy sets the rules for using an organization's systems, and users acknowledge it before getting access. A service level agreement defines a provider's performance promises, and a memorandum of understanding records a general agreement between organizations. A nondisclosure agreement covers protecting information, and a business continuity plan covers keeping operations going during a disruption.

questions.stem: Analysts cannot line up events across firewall, server and domain controller logs because the timestamps differ by several minutes. What fixes this?
options: Synchronizing every device to a common NTP time source
Lengthening the log retention period
Encrypting the logs in transit
Converting all logs to one file format
Hashing each log file once a day
questions.explain: Network Time Protocol keeps every device on the same clock, so events from different logs can be put in true order. Keeping logs longer, encrypting them or hashing them protects or preserves them but leaves the times wrong. A common file format helps parsing but does not correct the clocks.

questions.stem: Why is WEP considered broken and unfit for any network?
options: Its RC4 encryption uses a short 24-bit initialization vector, so the key can be recovered from captured traffic
It uses AES with a key that is too short
It depends on a RADIUS server that is easy to spoof
It encrypts only the network name, not the data
It works only on the 5 GHz band
questions.explain: WEP's 24-bit IV repeats quickly, and flaws in how it uses RC4 let attackers recover the key from enough captured packets, often in minutes. WEP never used AES, which came with WPA2. It does not need RADIUS, it does encrypt data frames, and it ran on 2.4 GHz networks.

questions.stem: What does the SAE handshake in WPA3-Personal improve over the pre-shared key handshake in WPA2-Personal?
options: It resists offline dictionary attacks against a captured handshake
It removes the need for any passphrase
It swaps AES for RC4 to run faster
It hides the network name from scanners
It requires every client to hold a certificate
questions.explain: With WPA2-Personal, an attacker who captures the four-way handshake can guess passphrases offline at high speed. SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) forces each guess to be a live exchange with the access point and adds forward secrecy. WPA3-Personal still uses a passphrase and AES, does not hide the SSID, and needs no client certificates.

questions.stem:
In Python, what does this code print?

a = 4
b = 7
a = a + b
b = a - b
a = a - b
print(a, b)
questions.explain: Trace one line at a time: a becomes 11, then b becomes 11 - 7 = 4, then a becomes 11 - 4 = 7. The three lines swap the values without a temporary variable. "11 4" stops one line early, and "4 7" assumes nothing changed.

questions.stem:
In Python, what does this code print?

x = 3
y = x
x = x * 2
y = y + x
print(y)
questions.explain: y = x copies the value 3; it does not link y to x. x then becomes 6, and y becomes 3 + 6 = 9. The answer 12 assumes y followed x up to 6 before the addition.

questions.stem:
In Python, what does this code print?

total = 0
for n in [2, 5, 8]:
    total = total * 2 + n
print(total)
questions.explain: Multiplication happens before addition on each pass: 0 * 2 + 2 = 2, then 2 * 2 + 5 = 9, then 9 * 2 + 8 = 26. 15 is just the sum of the list, and 52 doubles the total one extra time.

questions.stem:
In Python, what does this code print?

print(17 // 5 + 17 % 5)
questions.explain: // is integer (floor) division, so 17 // 5 = 3, and % gives the remainder, 17 % 5 = 2. 3 + 2 = 5. The answer 5.4 treats // as ordinary division (3.4) before adding the remainder.

questions.stem:
Using standard operator precedence, where ** is the exponent operator, what is the value of x?

x = 2 + 3 * 4 ** 2
questions.explain: Exponents come first: 4 ** 2 = 16. Then multiplication: 3 * 16 = 48. Then addition: 2 + 48 = 50. 80 adds before multiplying ((2 + 3) * 16), and 146 squares the product (2 + 12 ** 2).

questions.stem:
In JavaScript, what does this code print?

console.log(3 + 2 + "5" + 1);
questions.explain: + works left to right. 3 + 2 are both numbers, so they add to 5. 5 + "5" has a string, so it joins to "55", and "55" + 1 joins to "551". "3251" treats every + as joining, and 11 treats every + as adding.

options: B, then 0
A, then 0
B, then 5
A, then 5
An error, because = can't appear in a condition
questions.explain: A single = is assignment, not comparison. x = 0 stores 0 in x and the condition takes that value, 0, which counts as false, so the else branch prints B. x now holds 0. This is a classic bug: the comparison was meant to be x == 0 or x === 0.

questions.stem: In JavaScript, the remainder operator keeps the sign of the left number, so -3 % 2 is -1. Which condition is true exactly when the integer n is odd, including negative values?
options: Math.floor(n / 2) === n / 2
questions.explain: For any odd integer the remainder is 1 or -1, which is never 0, so n % 2 !== 0 catches both signs. n % 2 === 1 misses negative odd numbers like -3. The Math.floor test is true for even numbers, and n % 1 === 0 is true for every integer.

questions.stem: Which expression is always equivalent to NOT (A AND B)?
options: (NOT A) OR (NOT B)
(NOT A) AND (NOT B)
A OR B
(NOT A) OR B
(NOT A) AND B
questions.explain: De Morgan's law: negating an AND flips it to an OR and negates each part. NOT (A AND B) is false only when both are true, and so is (NOT A) OR (NOT B). (NOT A) AND (NOT B) is the negation of A OR B instead.

questions.stem:
For which values is this condition false?

(x > 5 and y < 3) or not (x > 5)
questions.explain: Whenever x is 5 or less, not (x > 5) is true, so the whole condition is true. With x = 6 the right side is false, and the left side needs y < 3; y = 3 fails it, so the condition is false. With x = 6, y = 2 the left side is true.

questions.stem:
The function hit() adds 1 to count and returns true. Languages with short-circuit evaluation stop checking an and/or as soon as the result is known. What is count after these three lines, if it starts at 0?

if (false and hit()) ...
if (true or hit()) ...
if (true and hit()) ...
options: It depends on what the if blocks do
questions.explain: false and anything is false, so hit() is skipped. true or anything is true, so hit() is skipped again. true and hit() still needs the right side, so hit() runs once. count ends at 1.

questions.stem: Access rule: allow entry if the user is an admin, or if the user is a member whose account is not locked. Which condition implements it?
options: isAdmin or (isMember and not isLocked)
(isAdmin or isMember) and not isLocked
isAdmin and isMember or not isLocked
not (isAdmin or isMember and isLocked)
isAdmin or isMember and isLocked
questions.explain: Admins get in regardless, so isAdmin stands alone on one side of the or. The member route needs both conditions together. (isAdmin or isMember) and not isLocked wrongly blocks a locked admin, and isAdmin and isMember or not isLocked lets in anyone who isn't locked.

options: D
B
C
F
Nothing, because grade is never assigned
questions.explain: An if/elif chain runs only the first branch whose test is true and skips the rest. 85 >= 60 is true, so grade is "D" and the later tests never run. The checks are in the wrong order for a grading scale: the highest threshold must be tested first.

x > 5 is true, so the inner test runs; x > 10 is false, so r = 2. The last if checks whether x is even; 7 % 2 is 1, so r stays 2. 20 assumes the even test passed, and 3 confuses the inner else with the outer one.

options: ABD
ABCD
AB
A
ACD
questions.explain: The three if statements are separate, so each is checked. 12 is even (A) and divisible by 3 (B). The elif belongs to the second if, which was true, so C is skipped even though 12 is divisible by 4. 12 > 10 adds D.
The values are 3, 7, 11, 15 and 19. The next value, 23, is past the stop, so the loop runs 5 times. 4 forgets 19, which is still below 20, and 17 is just 20 - 3.

questions.stem:
In Python, what does this code print?

i = 1
s = 0
while i < 10:
    s = s + i
    i = i * 3
print(s)
questions.explain: The condition is checked before each pass. i = 1 adds 1, i = 3 adds 3, i = 9 adds 9, then i becomes 27 and the test fails. s = 1 + 3 + 9 = 13. 40 wrongly adds 27, which is never added because the loop stops first.
The inner loop runs i times, and i takes the values 0, 1, 2 and 3. That is 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 passes. 16 assumes the inner loop always runs 4 times, and 10 includes an extra pass for i = 4.

continue skips multiples of 3 (3 and 6) but keeps looping; break ends the loop at k = 8. The values added are 1, 2, 4, 5 and 7, for 19. 27 ignores the break, and 3 treats continue as if it stopped the loop.

questions.stem: The list items has n elements, indexed 0 to n - 1. In this pseudocode, "for i = a to b" includes both a and b. Which loop causes an index-out-of-range error?
options: for i = 0 to n: print(items[i])
for i = 0 to n - 1: print(items[i])
for i = n - 1 down to 0: print(items[i])
for i = 1 to n: print(items[i - 1])
for i = 1 to n - 1: print(items[i])
questions.explain: Going from 0 to n inclusive reaches i = n, and items[n] is one past the last index, so it fails. The loop from 1 to n - 1 skips item 0 but never goes out of range. The other loops visit every valid index.

questions.stem:
In Python, what does this code print?

nums = [4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42]
print(nums[len(nums) - 2] + nums[1])
questions.explain: len(nums) is 6, so nums[4] is 23, the second-to-last item. Indexing starts at 0, so nums[1] is 8, not 4. 23 + 8 = 31. 24 counts positions from 1 (16 + 8), and 27 uses nums[0] for nums[1].

questions.stem:
In Python, a slice list[a:b] includes index a but stops before index b. What does this print?

letters = ["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"]
print(letters[1:4])
questions.explain: Index 1 is "b" because counting starts at 0. The slice takes indexes 1, 2 and 3 and stops before 4, giving b, c, d. ['b', 'c', 'd', 'e'] includes the stop index, and ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd'] counts from 1.

questions.stem:
In Python, what does this code print?

a = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
for i in range(1, len(a)):
    a[i] = a[i] + a[i - 1]
print(a[4])
questions.explain: Each element adds the already updated element before it, so the list becomes a running total: 1, 3, 6, 10, 15. 9 uses the original values (5 + 4), forgetting that a[3] was already changed to 10.

questions.stem: An array holds 250 elements and uses zero-based indexing. What is the index of its last element, and what happens when code reads index 250?
options: 249; the read is out of bounds and raises an error or returns an undefined value
250; the read returns the last element
249; the read wraps around and returns element 0
251; the read returns an empty value
250; the read is out of bounds and raises an error
questions.explain: With indexes starting at 0, 250 elements use indexes 0 to 249. Index 250 is one past the end, so most languages raise an error (Python, Java) and some return undefined (JavaScript). Arrays don't wrap around to the start.

questions.stem:
In Python, what does this code print?

def bump(n):
    n = n + 5
    return n

x = 10
bump(x)
y = bump(x)
print(x, y)
questions.explain: The function gets a copy of the number in x, so changing n never changes x. The first call's return value is thrown away. The second call returns 10 + 5 = 15. "15 20" assumes each call changed x permanently.

questions.stem:
In Python, what does this code print?

x = 1
def f():
    x = 2
    return x * 3

y = f()
print(x + y)
questions.explain: Assigning x inside f creates a new local variable; the global x stays 1. f returns 2 * 3 = 6, so x + y = 1 + 6 = 7. 8 assumes the function overwrote the global x with 2.

questions.stem:
In Python, what does this code print?

def area(w, h):
    return w * h

total = area(4, 9)

Which statement is correct?
options: w and h are parameters; 4 and 9 are the arguments passed to them
4 and 9 are parameters; w and h are the arguments
The function prints 36 when it is called
total holds the function area itself, not a number
w and h keep their values after the call ends
questions.explain: Parameters are the names in the function definition; arguments are the actual values in the call. The function returns 36, which is stored in total; it prints nothing. w and h are local and disappear when the call finishes.

options: False True
True False
True True
False False
3 True
questions.explain: return ends the function at once. For 9, d = 3 divides evenly, so it returns False. For 13, no d from 2 to 12 divides it, so the loop finishes and the function returns True. The function is a prime test.
Each call steps down by 2: f(7) = 7 * f(5) = 7 * 5 * f(3) = 7 * 5 * 3 * f(1), and f(1) is the base case, 1. That is 105. 5040 is 7 factorial, which steps down by 1, and 35 stops a call too early.

fib(4) calls fib(3) and fib(2); fib(3) calls fib(2) and fib(1); each fib(2) calls fib(1) and fib(0). That is fib(4) once, fib(3) once, fib(2) twice, fib(1) three times and fib(0) twice: 1 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 2 = 9. 4 counts one call per level, ignoring the repeated work.

questions.stem: A recursive function's base case is never reached for the input it is given. What happens when it runs?
options: It keeps calling itself until the call stack runs out of space, causing a stack overflow error
It loops forever without using extra memory, like an infinite while loop
It runs once and stops, because only loops can repeat
The compiler adds a base case automatically and returns 0
It returns the value of the last expression it evaluated
questions.explain: Every recursive call adds a frame to the call stack. With no base case to stop it, frames pile up until the stack's memory runs out and the program crashes with a stack overflow (Python reports a RecursionError). Unlike an infinite while loop, it does use more memory on every call.

questions.stem: A sorted list holds 1,000 names. What is the largest number of comparisons binary search needs to find a name or decide it isn't there?
questions.explain: Binary search halves the remaining range each time, so it needs about log2 of the size. 2 to the 10th is 1,024, which covers 1,000 items, so 10 comparisons is the worst case. 1,000 is the worst case for linear search, and 500 is linear search's average.

questions.stem: A correct binary search, which assumes the list is sorted, is run on the unsorted list [3, 9, 1, 7, 5] to look for 9. It checks the middle item and moves left or right. What happens?
options: It reports that 9 isn't in the list, even though it is
It finds 9 at index 1
It sorts the list first, then finds 9
It raises an error because the list is unsorted
It loops forever
questions.explain: The middle item is 1, which is less than 9, so the search keeps only the right half: 7 and 5. Both are less than 9, so the range empties and it reports not found. Binary search doesn't check that its input is sorted; it just gives a wrong answer.

questions.stem: Which operation takes constant time, O(1), on an array of n elements?
options: Reading the element at a given index
Finding the largest value in an unsorted array
Inserting a value at the front and shifting the rest
Searching for a value with linear search
Sorting the array with merge sort
questions.explain: An array stores elements in consecutive memory, so the address of any index can be computed directly, whatever n is. Finding the maximum and linear search must look at every element (O(n)), inserting at the front shifts n elements, and merge sort is O(n log n).

questions.stem: An algorithm compares every item with every other item, so its running time is O(n^2). It takes 2 seconds for 1,000 items. About how long will it take for 4,000 items?
options: 32 seconds
8 seconds
16 seconds
64 seconds
4 seconds
questions.explain: With O(n^2), multiplying n by 4 multiplies the work by 4^2 = 16. 2 seconds times 16 is 32 seconds. 8 seconds is what a linear O(n) algorithm would take.

questions.stem: Bubble sort compares each pair of neighbors from left to right and swaps them if the left one is larger. What is the list after the first full pass on [5, 1, 4, 2, 8]?
questions.explain: 5 and 1 swap, then 5 and 4 swap, then 5 and 2 swap, and 5 and 8 stay. The largest value bubbles to the end, giving [1, 4, 2, 5, 8]. The fully sorted list needs another pass, and [1, 5, 4, 2, 8] stops after the first swap.

questions.stem: A stack starts empty. These operations run in order: push 3, push 7, pop, push 2, push 9, pop, pop. In what order are values removed?
questions.explain: A stack is last in, first out. The first pop removes 7, the most recent push. After pushing 2 and 9, the next pops remove 9 and then 2, leaving 3 on the stack. "3, 7, 2" treats it as a first in, first out queue.

questions.stem: A queue starts empty. These operations run in order: enqueue A, enqueue B, enqueue C, dequeue, enqueue D, dequeue. Which item is now at the front?
options: C
D
B
A
The queue is empty
questions.explain: A queue is first in, first out. The two dequeues remove A and then B, the two oldest items. C and D remain, with C at the front. D would be the answer for a stack, where the newest item comes off first.

questions.stem:
In Python, what does this code print?

print(int("12") + float("0.5") * 2)
options: A TypeError, because the strings can't be added
questions.explain: int("12") converts the string to the integer 12, and float("0.5") to 0.5. Multiplication comes first: 0.5 * 2 = 1.0. Adding an int to a float gives a float, so the result is 13.0, not 13. 25.0 adds before multiplying.

A dictionary keeps one entry per unique key, so there are 3 keys: red, blue and green. get(w, 0) returns the current count or 0 for a new key, so red is counted 3 times. 6 confuses the number of keys with the number of words.

questions.stem: In most programming languages, 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 evaluates to false. Why?
options: Binary floating point can't store 0.1 and 0.2 exactly, so their sum is slightly off from 0.3
The == operator compares memory addresses, not values, for decimals
0.1 + 0.2 is rounded down to 0.2 by integer division
Decimal literals are stored as strings, so + joins them
The comparison happens before the addition
questions.explain: Like 1/3 in decimal, 0.1 has no exact binary form, so each value is stored as the nearest binary fraction. The sum is 0.30000000000000004, which isn't equal to the stored 0.3. Compare floats within a small tolerance instead of with ==.

options: ...Woof
WoofWoof
An error, because Puppy has no speak method
questions.explain: Puppy inherits from Dog, so it uses Dog's speak, which overrides Animal's. Each object runs the version that belongs to its own class, which is polymorphism. Animal() gives "..." and Puppy() gives "Woof". The nearest inherited method wins, not the one at the top.

questions.stem: A BankAccount class makes its balance field private. Code outside the class can change the balance only through deposit() and withdraw(), which reject negative amounts. Which principle is this?
options: Encapsulation
Inheritance
Polymorphism
Overloading
Instantiation
questions.explain: Encapsulation bundles data with the methods that act on it and hides the data so it can only change through controlled methods. Inheritance is a class taking on another class's members, polymorphism is one call running different versions, and instantiation is creating an object from a class.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts compiled and interpreted languages?
options: A compiler translates the whole program into machine code before it runs; an interpreter translates and runs it a statement at a time
An interpreter translates the whole program first; a compiler runs it a statement at a time
Compiled programs must be translated again every time they run
Interpreted programs can't have runtime errors, because each line is checked first
Only interpreted languages can be used to build web applications
questions.explain: A compiler does the translation once, ahead of time, and produces an executable that runs without it; C and C++ work this way. An interpreter reads and executes code as it goes, as in classic Python or JavaScript. Both kinds can hit runtime errors, and both are used on the web.

questions.stem: A program runs without crashing, but the average it reports is always a little too low, because it divides the total by n + 1 instead of n. What kind of error is this?
options: A logic error
A syntax error
A runtime error
A compile-time error
An overflow error
questions.explain: A logic error is code that is valid and runs but produces the wrong result. A syntax error breaks the language's grammar and stops the program from running at all, and a runtime error crashes the program while it runs, such as dividing by zero.

questions.stem: Which of these is a runtime error?
options: Dividing by a variable that holds 0 when the program runs
Leaving out a closing parenthesis
Using < where <= was intended
Spelling the keyword while as whlie
A loop that adds the wrong values to a total
questions.explain: A runtime error happens while the program is running, after it has been accepted as valid code: division by zero crashes at that moment. The missing parenthesis and the misspelled keyword are syntax errors, and < for <= and the wrong total are logic errors.

questions.stem: Using Git, a developer wants to try a risky change without disturbing the working main code, then add it to main if it works. Which sequence does this?
options: Create a branch, commit the changes on it, then merge the branch into main
Commit the changes to main, then create a branch to test them
Merge main into a new branch, then delete main
Clone the repository, push the change, then pull it back
Commit the changes to main and revert them if they fail
questions.explain: A branch is a separate line of development, so commits on it don't affect main. When the change works, merging brings those commits into main. Committing straight to main exposes everyone to the risky change, even if it can be reverted later.

questions.stem: Which HTML creates a link to https://example.com that opens in a new tab?
options: Example
Example
<link href="https://example.com" target="_blank">Example</link>
Example
Example
questions.explain: The anchor element <a> makes a link, href gives its address, and target="_blank" opens it in a new tab. src is for images and scripts, and <link> connects resources such as stylesheets in the page head; it doesn't create a clickable link. rel describes the relationship, not where the page opens.

questions.stem:
A page has this form, and the user types cats into the box and submits it. Which request is sent?

<form action="/search" method="get">
  <input name="q">
  <button>Go</button>
</form>
options: GET /search?q=cats
GET /search/cats
GET /search?input=cats
POST /search with q=cats in the body
GET /q?search=cats
questions.explain: With method="get", the browser adds the form fields to the action URL as a query string. Each field is sent as name=value, and the input's name is q, so the request is /search?q=cats. POST would put the fields in the request body instead.

options: Red
Blue
Green
Black, the browser default
Whichever color the last matching rule sets
questions.explain: When rules conflict, the more specific selector wins: an id beats a class, and a class beats an element name. #intro is the most specific, so the text is red. Order only decides between rules of equal specificity, so blue, set last, still loses.

questions.stem: A box has width: 200px; padding: 10px; border: 2px solid; margin: 20px; and the default box-sizing: content-box. How wide is the box from the outer edge of its left border to the outer edge of its right border?
options: 224px
200px
264px
212px
244px
questions.explain: With content-box, width sets the content only. Padding and border are added on both sides: 200 + 2 x 10 + 2 x 2 = 224px. Margin sits outside the border, so 264px (which adds 40px of margin) is the space the box takes up, not its border width.

questions.stem: Which selector matches only <li> elements that are direct children of a <ul> with the class menu?
options: ul.menu > li
ul .menu li
.menu li
ul.menu + li
ul > .menu li
questions.explain: ul.menu means a ul that has the class menu, and > means direct child. A space means any descendant, so .menu li would also match items in nested lists. + selects the next sibling, not a child, and ul .menu li looks for a menu element inside a ul.

questions.stem: A sign-up page uses JavaScript to reject passwords shorter than 12 characters before the form is submitted. Why must the server check the length again?
options: Client-side code runs on the user's machine, where it can be disabled or changed, so the server can't trust it
Browsers run JavaScript only after the form has been sent
JavaScript can't read the value of a password field
The server check makes the client check run faster next time
HTTP strips JavaScript out of every request for security
questions.explain: Anything in the browser is under the user's control: they can turn off scripts, edit the page or send a request with a tool, skipping the check entirely. Client checks are for convenience; the server must enforce every rule itself.
Each click runs both handlers in order. First click: 0 + 2 = 2, then 2 x 3 = 6. Second click: 6 + 2 = 8, then 8 x 3 = 24. 6 counts only one click, and 8 stops halfway through the second click.

questions.stem: A logged-in user requests a page that exists, but their account doesn't have permission to see it. Which status code fits best?
options: 403 Forbidden
401 Unauthorized
404 Not Found
500 Internal Server Error
301 Moved Permanently
questions.explain: 403 means the server knows who you are and refuses anyway. 401 means the request hasn't been authenticated, which doesn't fit a user who is already logged in. 404 means the resource doesn't exist, and 500 means the server itself failed.

questions.stem: A REST API stores user records at /users/42. Which method should a client use to replace that record completely with a new version?
options: PUT
GET
POST
HEAD
OPTIONS
questions.explain: PUT sends a complete representation to a specific address and replaces whatever is there; repeating it gives the same result. POST is normally used to create a new record in a collection, GET and HEAD only read, and OPTIONS asks which methods are allowed.

questions.stem: HTTP is stateless: each request stands on its own. How does a website usually keep a user logged in from one page to the next?
options: The server sets a cookie holding a session ID, and the browser sends it back with every later request
The server keeps the TCP connection open for as long as the user is on the site
The browser sends the username and password in the URL of every page
HTTP remembers the last user who connected from each IP address
The page's HTML stores the login, and links carry it along automatically
questions.explain: After login the server sends a Set-Cookie header with a session ID, and the browser includes that cookie on every request to the site, so the server can look up who it is. Connections close and IP addresses are shared, so neither identifies a user, and passwords never belong in URLs.

questions.stem: A browser requests an old URL and gets a 301 response. What should it do?
options: Request the new URL given in the Location header, and treat the move as permanent
Retry the same URL after a short wait
Show the user a page-not-found message
Report that the server crashed while building the page
Use the new URL this once, but keep requesting the old one in future
questions.explain: 3xx codes are redirects. 301 Moved Permanently gives the new address in the Location header, and browsers and search engines update to it. A temporary redirect, such as 302 or 307, is the one where the old URL stays in use.

questions.stem: Why should a login form use POST rather than GET?
options: GET puts the form fields in the URL, where they end up in browser history and server logs; POST sends them in the request body
POST encrypts the data, while GET sends it as plain text
GET can't send more than one form field at a time
POST requests are never stored by any server
GET requests can only be sent to the same server that served the page
questions.explain: A GET form adds fields to the URL, so a password would be saved in history, bookmarks and logs. POST keeps them in the body. POST does not encrypt anything; only HTTPS does that, so a login page needs both POST and HTTPS.

questions.stem:
Which statement correctly breaks down this URL?

https://shop.example.com:8443/items/view?id=77&color=red#reviews
options: Host shop.example.com, port 8443, path /items/view, query string id=77&color=red
Host example.com, port 8443, path /items/view?id=77, fragment color=red
Host shop.example.com, port 443, path /items/view, query string id=77
Host shop.example.com, port 8443, path /items, query string view?id=77&color=red
Host shop.example.com:8443, path /items/view, query string #reviews
questions.explain: The host comes after https:// and runs to the colon, the number after the colon is the port, and the path runs to the ?. The query string sits between ? and #, with pairs joined by &. #reviews is the fragment, which points to a spot on the page.

questions.stem:
Table Orders:
id | customer | total
1 | Ana | 40
2 | Ben | 75
3 | Ana | 90
4 | Cy | 60
5 | Ben | 20
6 | Ana | 55

What does this query return?

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Orders WHERE total > 50 AND customer <> 'Cy';
questions.explain: WHERE keeps rows where both conditions are true: total over 50 (rows 2, 3, 4 and 6) and customer not equal to Cy (which removes row 4). That leaves rows 2, 3 and 6. 4 ignores the customer condition.

questions.stem:
Table Orders:
id | customer | total
1 | Ana | 40
2 | Ben | 75
3 | Ana | 90
4 | Cy | 60
5 | Ben | 20
6 | Ana | 55

What does this query return?

SELECT customer FROM Orders ORDER BY total DESC LIMIT 2;
options: Ana, Ben
Ana, Ana
Ben, Cy
Ana, Cy
Ben, Ana
questions.explain: DESC sorts from largest to smallest total: 90 (Ana), 75 (Ben), 60 (Cy) and so on. LIMIT 2 keeps the first two rows, Ana then Ben. "Ben, Ana" keeps the right people in the wrong order, and "Ana, Cy" skips the 75.

questions.stem: Customers has id as its primary key. Orders has order_id as its primary key and a customer_id column that refers to Customers.id. Which statement is correct?
options: Orders.customer_id is a foreign key, and many orders can share the same customer_id value
Orders.customer_id must be unique, because it refers to a primary key
Customers.id is a foreign key that points to the Orders table
A primary key column can repeat values as long as some are NULL
Each customer can have only one order, because Customers.id is a primary key
questions.explain: A foreign key is a column that refers to another table's primary key, which links each order to a customer. The foreign key doesn't need to be unique, so one customer can have many orders. A primary key must be unique and can't be NULL.

questions.stem:
Customers:
id | name
1 | Ana
2 | Ben
3 | Cy

Orders:
id | customer_id
10 | 1
11 | 1
12 | 3
13 | 4

How many rows does this query return?

SELECT c.name FROM Customers c INNER JOIN Orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id;
questions.explain: An inner join returns one row for each pair that matches. Ana matches orders 10 and 11, Cy matches order 12, Ben matches none, and order 13's customer 4 doesn't exist. That is 3 rows. A left join would also keep Ben, giving 4, and 12 is every possible pairing.
